when-the-money-arrives-all-at-once.html: Sudden wealth rarely looks like a lottery ticket. More often it is an inheritance that arrives a decade early, the sale of a business you spent twenty years building, or a concentrated stock position that finally vests. Whatever the source, a lifetime of gradual saving becomes a single number in a bank account, and the decisions made in the next few months can matter more than the years that came before.

The first is doing nothing: parking everything in cash “until we figure it out”, sometimes for years. The second is the opposite: reinvesting or spending based on how the balance feels rather than what it needs to do. Both come from the same place. Nobody hands you a playbook when the money arrives.

when-the-money-arrives-all-at-once.text: Give yourself room before you commit

when-the-money-arrives-all-at-once.html: There is rarely a financial reason to make permanent decisions in the first ninety days. A short holding period lets you understand the tax picture, set aside what you will need in the next few years, and talk honestly with your family about what the money is for.

items: Set aside two to three years of planned spending in safe, liquid accounts.
Estimate the tax bill before you decide what is “left over”.
Write down what the money is for before deciding how to invest it.

when-the-money-arrives-all-at-once.html: The goal is not to decide quickly. It is to decide once, and well.
A good plan turns the number back into something you can live with: an income, a reserve, a gift, a legacy. That is the work worth doing first.

funding-your-trust.html: Many families sign a revocable trust and assume the job is done. But a trust only controls the assets that are actually titled to it. An unfunded trust can leave heirs facing the very probate process it was meant to avoid.

funding-your-trust.text: What usually belongs in the trust

items: Your home and other real estate
Interests in a closely held business
Valuable personal property with clear title

funding-your-trust.html: Retirement accounts such as IRAs and 401(k)s generally stay in your name and pass by beneficiary designation. Life insurance often does the same. The key is to coordinate those designations with the trust so the whole plan works together.
Funding is not a one-time event. Every new account or property is a chance to check that it is titled the way your plan intends.

the-estate-documents-that-matter-most.html: Estate planning conversations tend to start with wills and trusts. In practice, some of the most important documents are the ones that work while you are alive.

items: Health care power of attorney and advance directive

the-estate-documents-that-matter-most.html: A power of attorney lets someone you trust act for you if you cannot. Beneficiary designations often move more money than a will does. Both are simple to put in place and easy to forget.
Review your documents after every major life event, and at least every five years.

2026-market-and-economic-outlook.html: We enter the year with growth slowing but positive, inflation closer to target and bond yields well above where they started the decade. That combination argues for balance rather than bold bets.

items: Moderate economic growth with a low risk of a deep recession
Inflation settling in a range that allows gradual rate cuts
Equity returns closer to earnings growth than to last year’s gains

2026-market-and-economic-outlook.html: Portfolios stay close to long-term targets. We continue to favour high-quality businesses with durable earnings, and we have extended bond maturities modestly to lock in today’s yields.
As always, the best defence against an uncertain year is a plan built to survive one.

bonds-are-back.html: For most of the last decade, bonds were held for safety rather than income. With higher starting yields, high-quality fixed income can once again do both jobs.

bonds-are-back.text: Cash is a choice, not a default

bonds-are-back.html: Money market yields have been attractive, but they can fall quickly when rates are cut. For money not needed in the next two years, locking in yields for longer can make sense.
For clients in high tax brackets, municipal bonds often deliver more after tax than taxable alternatives. We compare the two on an after-tax basis for every portfolio.

donor-advised-funds-a-flexible-way-to-gi.html: A donor-advised fund lets you make a charitable contribution today, take the deduction in the year you give, and recommend grants to charities over time.

items: Bunching several years of giving into a high-income year
Donating appreciated stock instead of cash
Teaching children and grandchildren how to give with purpose

donor-advised-funds-a-flexible-way-to-gi.html: For many families, the fund becomes a shared project: a regular conversation about what matters and where the family wants to make a difference.

northstead-welcomes-rebecca-tran.html: Northstead Trust is pleased to welcome Rebecca Tran, CIMA®, as Investment Analyst. Rebecca joins from an investment consulting firm, where she spent six years on manager research and portfolio analytics.
At Northstead she supports the investment committee with equity research and due diligence, and produces our weekly market summary.

a-day-of-service-on-the-lakefront.html: Every summer our office closes for a day so the whole team can volunteer together. This year we joined a local conservation group on the lakefront, planting dune grass and clearing two miles of trail.
It is one of our favourite days of the year, and a reminder that the communities we serve are also the ones we live in.
